continents-1858.body: In 1858, the geographer Antonio Snider-Pellegrini noticed that the coasts of America and Africa fit together. He drew two globes: the continents joined, then apart. He explained the split by a catastrophe linked to the biblical Flood, and his idea went nowhere. More than half a century later, Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift, and science eventually confirmed that they had indeed formed a single landmass: Pangaea.
continents-1858.detail: On the left globe, the word written on America isn't "America" but "Atlantide", Atlantis.
continents-1858.credit: Antonio Snider-Pellegrini, 1858. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

egypt-ortelius.body: Abraham Ortelius, a mapmaker from Antwerp, published what is considered the first modern atlas in 1570. He gradually added maps of the ancient world, such as this one from 1584. So this isn't an Egyptian map: it is ancient Egypt as a Renaissance scholar reconstructed it from Greek and Roman authors. The Nile shapes the whole country, divided into provinces, the nomes, with their names in Latin.
egypt-ortelius.detail: At the bottom left, look for the pyramids and palm trees. At the top left, a medallion shows a plan of Alexandria.
egypt-ortelius.credit: Abraham Ortelius, 1584. Public domain, via Digital Commonwealth and Wikimedia Commons.

turin-papyrus.body: Drawn around 1150 BC, this papyrus is one of the oldest known geographical maps, and is often described as the oldest geological map. It is attributed to the scribe Amennakhte and linked to an expedition in the reign of Ramesses IV. It shows a valley in the Eastern Desert, the Wadi Hammamat, with its roads, stone quarries and gold deposits. Today it survives in fragments, kept at the Egyptian Museum in Turin.
turin-papyrus.detail: On the left, the pink part: these are the hills, coloured according to their rock. The rest of the roll is mostly text.
turin-papyrus.credit: Archivio Museo Egizio, Turin, C 1879 + C 1969 + C 1899. Image under CC0.

rome-395.body: In 395, on the death of Emperor Theodosius I, the Roman Empire was shared between his two sons: Honorius received the West, Arcadius the East. The division became permanent. The Western Empire disappeared in 476, while the Eastern one, also called Byzantine, lasted until 1453. This map was drawn in 1923 by the American historian William R. Shepherd: the Romans left none of this kind.
rome-395.detail: The colours show the empire's major divisions, and the list at the top right names its provinces. Find Constantinople, the capital of the East.
rome-395.credit: William R. Shepherd, Historical Atlas, 1923. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

caliphate-750.body: Within little more than a century of Muhammad's death in 632, the Arab conquests created an empire stretching from the Iberian Peninsula to the Indus. In 750, the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyad dynasty, and they soon founded a new capital, Baghdad. These conquests were imposed by force, but this area also became a great crossroads of trade and learning.
caliphate-750.detail: The three shades in the legend show the stages of the expansion: up to 632, up to 656, then up to 750. The dates on the map are those of the conquests.
caliphate-750.credit: William R. Shepherd, Historical Atlas, 1926 edition. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

holy-roman-empire.body: The Holy Roman Empire was not a unified country but a collection of duchies, principalities, bishoprics and towns under the often disputed authority of an emperor. Between 1138 and 1254, the Hohenstaufen dynasty led it, with figures such as Frederick Barbarossa and Frederick II. They also tried to dominate Italy, which set them against the popes and the Lombard towns. The dynasty eventually lost power, and the empire stayed fragmented.
holy-roman-empire.detail: Compare the north of the map, covered in duchies, with the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in the far south, which passed to the Hohenstaufen in 1194.
holy-roman-empire.credit: William R. Shepherd, Historical Atlas, 1926 edition. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

mongol-dominions.body: Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes in 1206. His successors built the largest contiguous empire in history, through extremely deadly conquests. By around 1300 it was already divided into four: the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhans of Persia and Yuan China. The routes it connected also eased exchanges between Asia and Europe.
mongol-dominions.detail: The red line marks the limits of the Mongol dominions around 1300. The grey area shows the empire ruled by Timur up to 1405.
mongol-dominions.credit: William R. Shepherd, Historical Atlas, 1923. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

tabula-rogeriana.body: In 1154, after some fifteen years of work, the Arab scholar al-Idrisi completed a description of the world for Roger II, the Norman king of Sicily. It brought together knowledge from the Muslim world and Europe, in 70 maps spread across seven climate zones. The original is lost. This version assembles the sections from surviving manuscripts: it is the reconstruction by the German researcher Konrad Miller, from the late 1920s.
tabula-rogeriana.detail: South is at the top. Turn the map over in your mind to find the Mediterranean and the shape of Italy.
tabula-rogeriana.credit: Al-Idrisi, 1154; reconstruction by Konrad Miller. Public domain, via the Library of Congress and Wikimedia Commons.

waldseemuller-1507.body: Printed in 1507, this map by Martin Waldseemüller is the first to use the name "America", in honour of the navigator Amerigo Vespucci. It also shows the new continent separated from Asia, before Europeans had even seen the Pacific Ocean. The only known copy was rediscovered in 1901 in a German castle. The Library of Congress bought it for 10 million dollars, in a sale completed in 2003.
waldseemuller-1507.detail: Look for the word "America" in the south of the new continent, then the portraits of Ptolemy and Vespucci at the top.
waldseemuller-1507.credit: Martin Waldseemüller, 1507. Public domain, via the Library of Congress and Wikimedia Commons.

ottoman-empire.body: In 1453, the Ottomans took Constantinople. Their empire then spread across three continents: Egypt and the holy places of Islam under Selim I, Hungary and Iraq under Suleiman the Magnificent. It brought together very diverse peoples, languages and religions, and many of these regions were subdued by war. In 1683, the failure before Vienna marked the start of its retreat in Europe.
ottoman-empire.detail: The legend follows the expansion in four colours, from 1481 to 1683. The dates are those of the conquests, and tributary states are in light pink.
ottoman-empire.credit: William R. Shepherd, Historical Atlas, 1923. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

russia-growth.body: Around 1300, the Principality of Moscow was a small territory paying tribute to the Golden Horde. In five centuries, its rulers extended it from the Baltic to the Urals and the Black Sea, often by war and at the expense of other peoples. Under Catherine II, Russia annexed Crimea and took part in the three partitions of Poland. This American map from 1923 uses the names of its time, such as "Little Russia" for part of Ukraine: these words and borders belong to the past, not to today.
russia-growth.detail: Find the small dark patch of Moscow around 1300, in the centre, then follow the legend's colours to the partitions of Poland, on the left.
russia-growth.credit: William R. Shepherd, Historical Atlas, 1923. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

british-empire-1886.body: This map is a propaganda poster. Published in 1886 in the newspaper The Graphic and illustrated by Walter Crane, it promotes the idea of a federation of the British Empire. The territories are in red, and the lines trace the sea routes. The words "freedom" and "fraternity" contrast with the reality of colonial rule, and colonised peoples are shown through the stereotypes of the time.
british-empire-1886.detail: At the bottom centre, Britannia sits enthroned on the world, surrounded by figures meant to represent the empire's peoples. Look at how they are shown.
british-empire-1886.credit: Walter Crane, 1886, statistics by J. C. R. Colomb. Public domain, via the Boston Public Library and Wikimedia Commons.
